extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of humor; communication professionals; psychologists; general readers interested in humor theory and the creative process
extracted.subtask_description: A methodology for analyzing and creating humor by isolating the technical mechanisms (techniques) that generate comic effect, then classifying and rating them to determine which are primary. Applicable across media, genres, and historical periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break down example into main elements (isolate techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of humor should involve breaking down the example of humor into its main elements or components—that is, isolating the various techniques used to generate the humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take any example of humor (in any time, genre, or medium) and identify the constituent techniques that together produce the humorous effect. This is the first analytic step before classification or evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate the techniques (primary vs. secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating the techniques—deciding which technique is basic and which techniques are secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After isolating techniques, decide which mechanism is dominant in producing the humor and which are supporting. The relative prominence of techniques affects interpretation and how one might reproduce or alter the humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four basic categories of humor (language, logic, identity, action)
rubrics_metrics.description: All techniques of humor can be subsumed under four basic categories: Language (verbal), Logic (ideational), Identity (existential), and Action (physical or nonverbal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to get a sense of what kind of humor is being produced (e.g., verbal wit vs. physical slapstick). Note that techniques themselves are the essential analytic units; categories are organizational aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques should be treated as comprehensive and mutually exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed techniques were elicited by content analysis and are intended to be comprehensive and mutually exclusive classification elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on techniques rather than traditional forms/genres: e.g., treat parody as a technique rather than a form. This approach privileges functional mechanisms over subject matter or form when analysing humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of joke as form (and caution about telling jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is defined as a story with a punch line that is used for comic effect. Telling jokes is typically performing someone else’s material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cautions that telling others' jokes is generally not the best route to being funny; instead, creators should use the catalogued techniques to generate original humor. (Subtitle idea: 'How To Be Funny Without Telling Jokes for Those Who Tell Jokes Without Being Funny.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reversals of techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: When analysing or generating humor we must consider reversals of techniques (e.g., understatement as the reverse of exaggeration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals often function similarly but in opposite directions; analysing both a technique and its negative form can reveal a fuller set of comic possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity, confusion, and nonsense (logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity and related forms (confusion and nonsense) produce humor by making light of traditional demands of logic and rationality; effects can range from silly to philosophically sophisticated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Buffalo 'two other fellows' exchange; elephants painting toenails red to hide in cherry trees; the herring/towel exchange. Mechanisms include subverting expectation, redirecting attention from ridiculous premises to their 'proved' truth, and exploiting probability/impossibility to elicit puzzlement or amusement. Often tied to existential or absurdist art (e.g., Beckett, Ionesco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident (logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidents generate humor from slips of the tongue, typographical errors, ambiguous sentence constructions, or other chance occurrences; distinct from mistakes and coincidences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: garbled headlines ('Thugs Eat/ Then Rob Proprietor'), mispunctuated ads ('Sheer stockings—designed for dressy wear, but so serviceable that many women wear nothing else.'). Distinguish: an accident is chance-based; a mistake/error stems from ignorance or imprudence; a coincidence is a chance correspondence that may embarrass. Accidents are humorous when not serious or anxiety-provoking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusions (language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusions rely on shared cultural, social, political, or sexual references; they cue recall of well-known events, scandals, traits, or tropes and produce humor by invoking that shared knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the honeymooning Lieutenant whose 'it' is misinterpreted; the troupe advertising Shakespeare plays with clues tied to sexual phenomena. Allusions are 'consensual'—they work because the audience shares the referent and the matter is not so serious as to cause pain. Allusions often intersect with mistakes, gaffes, and social information.
